summary: Defines the 608 Rejected response code for the Session Initiation Protocol. It tells a caller that an intermediary, such as an analytics engine, rejected the call so it will not be delivered. As a 6xx code, it signals that retrying the same user agent is likely to fail.

eli5.summary: When a phone call is blocked by a spam filter, this gives the caller a clear message that the call was rejected on the way.

questions: how sip tells caller call was blocked
what is the sip.608 feature capability
subtitle: A SIP response code that tells a caller an intermediary, not the person called, rejected the call, with a signed way to appeal.

tldr.problem: When an analytics engine or other intermediary blocks a call as unwanted, SIP has no way to say that a machine, not the called person, made the decision, or to let a wrongly blocked caller contact whoever blocked them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8688 defines the 608 (Rejected) response code. The intermediary may attach a Call-Info header with purpose jwscard, pointing to a signed JSON Web Signature of a jCard that holds redress contact details. A sip.608 feature capability and an announcement cover callers whose equipment does not understand 608.
tldr.outcome: Callers can learn who rejected the call and how to appeal, while the called party's own contact details stay hidden. As a 6xx code, it also tells the caller that retrying the same user agent will likely fail.

facts.label: Required jCard properties
facts.value: At least one of URL, EMAIL, TEL, ADR

today: RFC 8688 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2019, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines 608 alongside the 607 code of RFC 8197.

sections.title: The Problem with Unexplained Blocking
sections.content:
The IETF has been working on unwanted and sometimes illegal calls. STIR and SHAKEN address signing and attestation of the caller identity. RFC 8688 adds a Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) response code, 608, that lets a calling party learn an intermediary rejected the call. No one will deliver, and so answer, the call.

A distinct indicator matters because in some jurisdictions a service provider may not be allowed to block calls without an explicit user request, or may be allowed only if a remediation mechanism exists for false positives. Users can also misidentify callers: a legitimate caller may be marked illegal, and an analytics engine may then block that source for everyone.

Existing options fit poorly. A blocking service might answer 604 (Does Not Exist Anywhere), but other network elements may take that to mean the user truly does not exist, and the RFC notes that such false signaling is illegal in many jurisdictions.
sections.eli5: A caller who is turned away deserves to know that a filter did it, and who to ask if the filter was wrong.

sections.title: Why Not Reuse 607
sections.content:
RFC 8197 defines 607 (Unwanted), which a human user sends to say they do not want a call. The proxy can pass that on to a call analytics engine, and the caller learns the user is not interested.

An intermediary could in principle use 607 too, but downstream elements might treat it as a human judgment. An algorithm using statistics or machine learning can fall victim to the base-rate fallacy, so a 608 lets downstream analytics weigh a machine rejection differently, or decide whether to consider it at all.

Putting alternate contact details in a 607 would also be counterproductive, since most blocked calls really are illegal and a user's contact details should not be handed to them. And the called party's relationship is with the analytics provider, not the caller, so the caller needs a way to reach the intermediary's operator without exposing the target user's contact information.
sections.eli5: A person saying "no thanks" and a robot saying "no thanks" should look different, so everyone can tell which one it was.

sections.title: How the Intermediary Rejects a Call
sections.content:
An intermediary here is the entity acting as a SIP user agent server on the user's behalf, either a back-to-back user agent or a proxy. It MAY send 608 in a failure response to an INVITE, MESSAGE, SUBSCRIBE or other out-of-dialog request, and MAY use 608 as the cause value in a Reason header field.

If there are no indications that the caller will misuse it, the intermediary MUST include a Call-Info header field. Its purpose parameter MUST be jwscard, and its value MUST refer to a JWS encoding of a jCard. A proxy that sees a 608 while other paths are in progress follows the usual 6xx rules from RFC 3261: cancel pending transactions and create no new branches.

The examples in the RFC are marked as non-normative and possibly containing errors, so the numbered text is the reference.
sections.eli5: The guard writes a note saying "I turned you away, and here is who to talk to," and slips it back to the caller.

sections.title: The Signed jCard
sections.content:
The redress contact is a jCard (the JSON form of vCard) wrapped in a JSON Web Signature, so it carries its own integrity protection. The JOSE header MUST include typ, alg and x5u. The typ MUST be vcard+json, implementations MUST support ES256 and MAY support other registered algorithms, and x5u MUST be a URI that resolves to the public key certificate for the signing key.

The payload has two claims. The iat (issued at) claim MUST be set to the time of the 608 response and protects against replay. The jcard claim holds the jCard and MUST contain at least one of the URL, EMAIL, TEL or ADR properties. What the intermediary does when contacted is out of scope.

The RFC says implementations MUST NOT insert line breaks into the base64url encodings of the header or token, and receivers MUST be ready for pretty-printed, compact or oddly formatted JSON of arbitrary length.
sections.eli5: The note carries a stamp that only the real guard has. The stamp has a time on it, so an old note cannot be reused.

sections.title: What the Caller's Side Must Do
sections.content:
A conforming UAC MUST include the sip.608 feature-capability indicator in a Feature-Caps header field of its INVITE. On receiving a 608 it does normal SIP processing for 6xx responses. It MUST check the iat claim and reject jCards with an expired value. What counts as expired is local policy, with something on the order of a minute suggested because of clock drift and a possible audio announcement before the response.

The Security Considerations also suggest the caller can use the signature and the signing certificate, for example checking that the certificate subject relates to the To header field of the original request, to decide whether to trust the contact information.
sections.eli5: The caller says up front that it understands these notes, and checks the time stamp before trusting one.

sections.title: Callers That Do Not Understand 608
sections.content:
A caller from a legacy network, reached through a media gateway, will not understand 608. The first network element that conforms to this specification therefore inserts the sip.608 feature capability (per RFC 6809) and takes on the job of playing an announcement saying at least how to contact the operator of the intermediary. If the INVITE has no sip.608 indicator, the intermediary acts as if it had inserted one and MUST play the announcement, subject to the caveats on security. The element MUST still forward the 608 as the final response to the INVITE.

To play audio before a final failure, the element MUST use a 183 Session Progress response. The UAC MUST include support for 100rel in its INVITE, the element MUST require it in the 183, the UAC MUST send a PRACK and the element MUST answer with 200 OK PRACK. The announcement should match the requested media: audio for an audio-only INVITE, or text if the INVITE only asked for real-time text and the element can render it. A call center that controls both the legacy callers and a modern outbound proxy can instead handle the Call-Info digitally.
sections.eli5: If the caller cannot read the note, the first helper who can read it reads it aloud over the phone, then still passes the note along.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists several risks. A truly malicious caller learns it is being automatically blocked and gets a contact point to attack, so operators may wish to include Call-Info only for requests that pass STIR validation. An attacker could also abuse the announcement as an amplification attack, since an INVITE can be under 1 kilobyte and an audio file hundreds of kilobytes, by pointing the SDP at a victim. The suggested remedy is to play media only for a STIR-signed INVITE that validates, plus connectivity checks such as those in RFC 8445.

A malicious or spoofed 608 could point callers to a phishing contact, or direct many callers at a victim address. Signing the jCard lets the caller trace and verify the sender. If the intermediary encodes per-call information in the URI, it MUST use a non-deterministic URI reference and be ready to return dummy responses for calls that do not exist, so guessing URIs reveals nothing. Whether to include Call-Info at all is a policy choice, since in some jurisdictions the caller can already work out the terminating provider.
sections.eli5: A note with a phone number can be faked or misused, so it is signed, and the helper only reads it aloud to people who proved who they are.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC makes four registrations. It adds SIP response code 608 (Rejected) to the Response Codes registry, the feature-capability indicator sip.608 to the SIP Feature-Capability Indicator Registration Tree, the JSON Web Token claim jcard (jCard data) with the IESG as change controller, and the predefined value jwscard for the purpose parameter of the Call-Info header field.
sections.eli5: The new names are written in the official lists so everyone uses them the same way.
